result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.global_efficiency()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the global efficiency of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L37824-L37915){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.global_efficiency() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Global efficiency](/assets/graphs/global-efficiency.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph and a card that groups its 15 node pairs by distance and adds one over the distance for each: 6 pairs at 1, 6 at one half, 2 at one third, 1 at one quarter, 9.917 in all. Divided by 15 pairs this gives efficiency 0.661." width="100%"} Global efficiency is the average efficiency over pairs of nodes, where efficiency is the multiplicative inverse of the shortest path distance. It measures how efficiently information flows through the network: nodes one hop apart contribute `1`, nodes two hops apart contribute `1/2`, and so on. A graph where every node is close to every other scores near `1`; long chains score low. Global efficiency is a popular summary of network integration, for example to: - compare how well different network designs (transport, communication, brain connectivity) support fast communication - measure robustness by tracking how efficiency drops as nodes or edges are removed - compare graphs of different sizes on a common `[0, 1]` scale Distances are hop counts from a breadth-first search; edge weights are ignored. In a directed graph, distances follow edge direction, so each ordered pair `(u, v)` is considered separately. Every node is used as a source, so the cost is one BFS per node, which can be slow on very large graphs. Unreachable pairs count as efficiency `0` (their distance is infinite), and the average is taken over all `n(n-1)` ordered pairs of distinct nodes, so splitting a graph into disconnected pieces lowers its efficiency. This matches the standard definition and NetworkX's `global_efficiency()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The global efficiency, between `0` and `1`. Graphs with fewer than two nodes, or with no edges, return `0.0`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Latora and Marchiori (2001) introduced global efficiency as an information-flow measure on a comparable $[0, 1]$ scale across any topology: $E = \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i \ne j} \dfrac{1}{d(i, j)}$, with $1/d(i, j) = 0$ when $j$ is unreachable from $i$. Using $1/d$ rather than $d$ is what keeps the measure finite on disconnected graphs, where the mean shortest path is undefined. A complete graph achieves the maximum of $1$. The computation runs an unweighted BFS from every node, so cost is $O(V(V + E))$ time and $O(V)$ extra space per source. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A complete graph has every pair of nodes directly connected, so its global efficiency is at its maximum of 1: ::: {#c438f198 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_full_graph(5) # Returns 1.0 graph.global_efficiency() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: Sparser topologies have longer average shortest paths and therefore lower efficiency; a star graph is more efficient than a path of the same size, since every node is at most 2 hops from any other through the hub: ::: {#a51b9e99 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(10) star = ec.Graph() star.add_star_graph(10) # Path efficiency is lower than star efficiency (path.global_efficiency(), star.global_efficiency()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (0.4286596119929453, 0.6) ``` ::: ::: Unreachable pairs count as `0`. With two separate edges, only 4 of the 12 ordered node pairs can reach each other (each at distance 1), so the efficiency is `4 / 12`, about `0.333`, rather than `1.0`: ::: {#b8362b04 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} split = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "D")]) ) split.global_efficiency() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.3333333333333333 ``` ::: :::
